title: How to Do a Spending Audit in One Afternoon
description: How to do a spending audit: guess first, pull three months of statements, sort every purchase into categories, and find the gaps worth fixing.
figureLabel: a month you did not notice
keywords: spending audit how to do a spending audit where does my money go track spending categories
takeaways: Guess your spending first, then compare it with three months of real statements.
The gaps between guess and reality are your findings, usually two or three categories.
Pick one or two changes and give the money you free up a job straight away.
body:
If your money seems to vanish between payday and the end of the month, you are not alone, and you are probably not careless. Most spending now is small, quick, and easy to forget: a tap here, an automatic charge there. A spending audit sorts that out. It is a one-time look backward at what you actually spent over the last three months, grouped into categories, so you can see real numbers instead of guesses. This is not a budget, and it is not a monthly routine. If you already keep up a regular check-in with your money, that habit is covered in [the 20-minute monthly money review](/blog/monthly-money-review/). An audit is the step that comes before it. You do it once, it takes an afternoon, and it shows you where the money really went. Most people who try it find at least one surprise. ## What a spending audit actually is An audit sounds serious, like something an accountant does to a business. Yours is much simpler. You take your real transactions from the last three months, group them into categories like groceries, eating out, transport, and subscriptions, and add each group up. Then you compare those totals with what you thought you were spending. The gaps between the two are the whole point of the exercise. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau makes the same point in its Your Money, Your Goals toolkit: people who track their spending often discover they are spending money in small ways that add up, sometimes in ways that do not match their priorities. Small is the key word. Big bills are hard to miss. It is the $9 and $14 charges that slip past, week after week. An audit is not about feeling bad, and it is not about cutting everything fun out of your life. It is about swapping a vague worry, "I spend too much somewhere," for a specific fact, "I spend $264 a month on eating out." Facts are far easier to act on than worries. ## What you need before you start You need three things: your statements, somewhere to add things up, and roughly two hours when nobody will interrupt you. For statements, download or open the last three months from every place money leaves: your main bank account, any credit cards, and any payment apps you actually spend from, such as PayPal, Venmo, or Cash App. Miss one account and your totals will be wrong in exactly the place you were not looking. For adding up, use whatever you will actually finish with. A notebook works. A spreadsheet works better, because it does the math for you and nothing gets lost. If you want the sorting done for you, there is a free worksheet that matches this guide, with the categories and totals already set up, so you can fill in your own numbers as you go.

Download the free Spending Audit Worksheet (.xlsx)

It works in Google Sheets and Excel. No sign-up needed. ![The spending audit worksheet comparing guesses with real spending for each category](/assets/img/posts/spending-audit-worksheet-preview-1280x747.webp) One more thing: a pen and a blank page for Step 1. Do not skip it. It feels like a game, but it is the part that makes the whole audit stick in your head. ## Step 1: Write down your guesses first Before you open a single statement, write down what you think you spent last month in each category. Groceries. Eating out. Subscriptions. Transport. Shopping. Fun money. Fees. Guess quickly and do not look anything up. Round numbers are fine. Almost everyone guesses low on the small, frequent categories and about right on the big fixed ones. Rent is rent; you know that number cold. Coffee, snacks, deliveries, and little online orders are where memory gets generous with itself. Keep the page. In Step 4 you will set your guesses next to the real totals, and that side by side view is the moment the audit pays off. Writing it down matters more than it sounds. A 2023 study written up by University of Illinois Extension found that mentally sorting and tracking expenses is linked with higher financial well-being. Guessing first, then checking, is the fastest way in. ## Step 2: Pull three months of statements Why three months? One month can lie to you. Maybe that month held a birthday, a car repair, or a holiday, and none of that is your normal life. Twelve months tells the full truth, but it takes so long that most people quit halfway through, and a half-finished audit helps nobody. Three months is the middle ground: long enough to smooth out one odd month, short enough to finish in an afternoon. Work account by account. If your bank lets you download your transactions as a spreadsheet file, often called a CSV, take it. Scrolling through statements on screen works too, it just takes longer. While you work, note any charge you do not recognize at all. Do not stop to investigate it yet. Put a star beside it and keep moving. You will deal with all the starred charges together at the end. ## Step 3: Sort everything into simple categories Now sort every transaction into a category. Keep the list short, around ten categories. More than that and you will spend your afternoon arguing with yourself about whether a pharmacy run counts as groceries or health, and that argument helps no one. A set that works for most people: housing and bills, groceries, eating out and coffee, transport, subscriptions, shopping, fun and going out, health, fees and interest, and everything else. Three sorting rules will save you a lot of pain: - Do not judge while you sort. Place each charge, then move on. Judging as you go slows you down and makes you want to stop. - Count credit card purchases, not the card payment. If you also count the payment as spending, you count the same money twice. Interest and card fees are real costs, though, so put those in the fees category. - For cash, do your best and move on. Money you took out of an ATM and cannot account for goes in "everything else." If that pile ends up big, that is a finding all by itself. Shared spending counts too, but only your share of it, the part that actually left your account. If splitting costs with the people you live with gets messy, [how to split bills with roommates](/blog/how-to-split-bills-with-roommates/) has a fair way to divide things up. ## Step 4: Compare your guesses with the real numbers Add up each category across the three months and divide by three. That gives you your real monthly average. Now set it next to your guesses from Step 1 and look at the difference. Here is what that can look like. This is an illustration with made up numbers, for someone taking home about $2,400 a month: | Category | Your guess | Actual average | Difference | |-----------------------|------------|----------------|------------| | Groceries | $300 | $385 | $85 more | | Eating out and coffee | $120 | $264 | $144 more | | Subscriptions | $30 | $67 | $37 more | | Transport | $180 | $205 | $25 more | | Shopping | $100 | $172 | $72 more | | Fees and interest | $0 | $23 | $23 more | | Total | $730 | $1,116 | $386 more | Read the difference column slowly. The total gap in this example is $386 a month. Over a year, that comes to $4,632. Nobody sat down and decided to spend that. It leaked out in amounts too small to notice one at a time. Your numbers will be different, and that is fine. Maybe your gap is $80. Maybe your groceries guess was spot on and transport is the shock. Whatever your two or three biggest gaps are, those are your findings. Everything else the audit turned up is background. ## Step 5: Look closely at the usual hiding spots Before you decide what to change, scan your sorted lists once more for four things that hide well. ### Recurring charges Anything that bills you monthly or yearly at the same amount. Add them up as a total of their own; people are often surprised by that single number. If you find services you have not opened in a month, that is money you can stop sending out today, and [how to cancel subscriptions you don't use](/blog/cancel-subscriptions/) walks through cancelling them the right way. ### Fees and interest Overdraft fees, late fees, card interest, out-of-network ATM charges. On their own they feel like bad luck. On a statement they form a pattern, and patterns can be changed. ### Food away from home Not just meals out with friends. Delivery fees, tips, the coffee on the way to work, the snack at the register. In a lot of audits this is the single biggest gap between the guess and the truth, because no one purchase feels like a real decision. ### Charges you do not recognize Now go back to the starred ones. Most turn out to be a forgotten free trial or a company billing under a different name than the one on the storefront. A few are genuine errors. It is worth a phone call about those, because banks and card companies do fix mistakes when you point at them. ## Step 6: Pick only three fixes This is where most audits die. People find ten problems, try to fix all ten on Monday morning, and give up by Friday. So pick three. Only three. Choose the ones that save real money without making your daily life miserable. Using the example above, a sensible three would look like this: 1. Cancel two subscriptions that overlap or go unused. That saves $28 a month. 2. Cap eating out at $180 a month instead of $264. That saves $84 a month. 3. Together that is $112 a month, or $1,344 over a year. Then give that money a job before it quietly evaporates somewhere else. Set up an automatic transfer for the day after payday, even if it starts small. If you have no cushion at all, that job is an emergency fund. The Federal Reserve's Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2024 report found that 63 percent of adults said they would cover a $400 emergency expense using cash or its equivalent, which means a lot of people could not. A starter cushion puts you ahead of that. [How to build an emergency fund on a small income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/) shows how to build one when money is tight. ## After the audit: turn your findings into a simple budget An audit tells you the truth about the past. A budget is how you use that truth next month. Take your real category averages, trim the three things you chose in Step 6, and leave the rest as they are. What you get is a budget built on your actual life instead of hopeful numbers copied from the internet, and budgets built on guesses tend to fall apart within a few weeks. If you want the basics laid out plainly, [how to budget on less than $1,000 a month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) goes through them step by step. You do not need to repeat the full audit often. Once a year is plenty for most people, or right after a big change such as a new job, a move, or a new baby. In between, a light monthly check-in keeps you honest without another afternoon of sorting. ## Frequently asked questions ### How long does a spending audit take? About two hours the first time, if you download your transactions instead of scrolling through statements page by page. You can split it over two evenings if that suits you better. Just finish the sorting before you start changing anything, so your decisions rest on the full picture. ### How far back should I go? Three months is the sweet spot for most people. One month is too easy to distort with a single unusual bill. Twelve months is more complete, but most people abandon it partway, and an audit you finish beats a perfect one you quit. ### What if I spend a lot of money in cash? Count what you can from receipts and your banking app, and put untracked ATM withdrawals in their own line so you can see the size of the blind spot. If that line is big, carry a small notebook or use a notes app for one month and write down every cash purchase. The habit is annoying for about three days, then it gets interesting. ### Should I count bills I share with other people? Count your share only, meaning the amount that actually leaves your account. Counting the full rent when you pay half of it will throw every total off and make your housing look worse than it is. ### Do I need an app to do this? No. Paper, a spreadsheet, and most budgeting apps can all hold the same numbers. The audit works because you looked at your spending closely, not because of the tool you used to look at it. ## A quick note This article is general information to help you understand your own spending. It is not personal financial advice. If your situation involves serious debt, legal trouble, or tax problems, talk to a qualified professional or a free nonprofit money advice service in your country before acting. ## Sources - [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Your Money, Your Goals: Spending Tracker](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_your-money-your-goals_spending_tracker_2018-11_ADA.pdf) - [Federal Reserve Board, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2024 (press release, May 2025)](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/other20250528a.htm) - [University of Illinois Extension, Try Daily Expense Tracking (August 2026)](https://extension.illinois.edu/blogs/finding-financial-balance/2026-08-31-try-daily-expense-tracking)
